doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Mother's illness; first drum lessons from a WPA drummer
summary: After his mother's death at his age 14, he sees a WPA band drummer, learns to play along to Goodman and Krupa records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: that he went to Handy — W.C. Handy’s music store there in Nashville, Tennessee. Now my dad was born what, in the 1890s, so that had to be what, the early 1900s. He used to tell me that story. And my dad played ukulele and he sang and he would sing “Waiting for Ships that Never Come In” and they would do the recitations. Oh yeah. That’s when people would visit. Because the big thing then was visiting in various homes and entertaining. And my mother — on my father’s side my grandfather was a preacher. He was ordained. And so she had the chance, she was educated and played the piano. She was trained. You’d put the music up in front of her and she’d read it. So what happened, oh I was very young and my mother would try to get me to play the piano. But me, no. She was going to teach me. So I’d get down there, and fiddling, but no, I wanted to go out and play cowboys and Indians. I’ve kicked myself a million times. But what happened, my mother, when I was ten years old, she became ill and they took her to a hospital and she was in the hospital for two years. So then from twelve to fourteen she was at home. So there was really nobody to really do any encouraging. And then she passed away, see, so I was fourteen years old and my dad, he worked, and then he broke up the house and I was boarded out. So I can say that there was encouragement on my mother’s side but I blew it. So after that, oh we kids would play. Several had a piano and when I’d go different friends we’d bang on the piano — “Chopsticks” — and just do a lot of foolish stuff. And one time I went to a teenage dance. And this was in the thirties, mid to late-thirties. And the WPA at that time, they had a music project. And they would send out different groups to play for the youth centers and oh, elderly, places for the elderly. So I went to this teenage dance and there they had a band. The WPA band. And the drummer was setting up and he had the foot, and the hi-hat going, and in the meantime he was putting stuff together. And I’m going how in the world can you do the different beats with each foot, separately but together? And he said, “Well what do you think? Do you think you could do that? Would you like to learn?” I said, “Sure.” So he was a doorman on Pacific Heights with a split shift, and during his split he would come home, right there in the Western Addition. And I lived close to him. So he told me where he lived, told me to come by. So I went by and he put on his — he had an electric phonograph, so he puts on the Benny Goodman Trio, “Tea for Two,” with Gene Krupa. And I listened. And so he said, “What do you think, do you think you could play to that record?” So I tried to keep the foot going and tried to get the sound that I heard Krupa doing. And he says, “Well maybe we can make something out of you.” So that’s what I would do. I would take lessons from him. And then I joined the union. Well what happened, then I would hang out — Vernon Alley and Eddie Alley, are two brothers here, they, along with Wesley Peoples, they formed a band. And so Wesley is a fine pianist.
